utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General Fraser.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday at transcript page 5821 we started to talk about paragraph 27 of your consolidated statement, P576, page 12 in English, page 13 in the B/C/S. I believe you still have a copy in front of you for your own use, and I'd like to start off there again. And first of all I'd like to ask you, yesterday, at transcript page 5785, you talked with Ms. Bolton about a tunnel at Donji Kotorac where UNPROFOR had a check-point 200 metres away and UN personnel traversed in front of it, the entrance to the tunnel frequently. Is that tunnel that you talked about yesterday the same tunnel that you described in paragraph 27 of your statement as being used by both civilian and ABiH traffic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this tunnel pre-existing or was it something that was dug or constructed while UNPROFOR was -- was present?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it was there when I arrived. I couldn't tell you before when it was constructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What knowledge did UNPROFOR have of weapons or ammunition being shipped via that tunnel to the ABiH forces inside of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that it was used by both the military and civilians; but other details than that, I don't have any firm recollection at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR ever protest to the Bosnian Muslim side about the use of this airport tunnel for the transport of ABiH forces' supplies, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something that was very sensitive with UNPROFOR, and we did talk to both sides about the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did UNPROFOR ever try to keep track of the amounts and types of material that were brought in by this route?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did the best of our ability to keep the tunnel under observation, but you can appreciate the Muslims didn't want us to see very much about the tunnel, and so we just tried to watch what was going through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there a suspicion that some black marketeering was going on with respect to the tunnel, in particular, with respect to Brigadier Fikret?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of black marketeering in general. We were aware of Fikret and his activities, and we had conversations with Muslim authorities about both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so you can clarify for us, Brigadier Fikret, was he a commander of the ABiH forces around the airport?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the BiH forces just on that other side of the airport that went up into the Igman Mounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such a tunnel and any road used to transport military personnel or military supplies, or weapons, was a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was complicated by the fact that it was also for civilian use.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Brigadier Fikret was essentially a criminal thug who operated with a degree of independence and rose to be a division commander in the ABiH by the end of your tour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that three questions in one or ... I see a criminal, degree of independence, and how he rose. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll break it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Brigadier Fikret was essentially a criminal thug?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of his criminal activities, and we protested against those criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that he operated with a degree of independence within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We noted his latitude of action and commented on that with Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, if you know, is it correct that he rose to be a division commander within the ABiH by the end of your tour in -- at Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something I -- I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 5791, you were asked about UNMOs. I would like to take a look at paragraph 28 and 29 of your statement; again, that's P576 and we should still be on page 10 in the English and page 11 in the Serbian. And here in these paragraphs you are talking about the UNMO relationship vis-a-vis UNPROFOR. First of all, sir, could you tell us, if you recall, who the SMO of the UNMO mission in Sarajevo was during the period of your deployment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Roy Thomas was there for a large part of my tour, another Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document now, 65 ter number 1D423, and if at first we can have the first page of that document in e-court. And, sir, as you could see from -- this first page of this document purports to be an information report from a proofing session between General Sir Michael Rose and the Office of the Prosecutor. And it says that it's: "Information provided by General Sir Michael Rose to Mark Ierace, Chester Stamp, Jonathan Tait-Harris, Richard Philipps on 29 August 2003 at Ministry of Defence, London, United Kingdom." If we could turn to page 4 in e-court of this proofing note, I'd like to ask you about something General Rose says about the UNMO mission. And here he says: "The UNMO reports" --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are you so I can just follow along?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be page 4, but I'm not seeing ... Ah, the last paragraph, sir, of the English version which is on the right side of your screen. "The UNMO reports were completely useless. It was a money spinner. They wrote shootreps and reports based on what they were told by the local commanders. Mainly were not technically competent and some were sold out. They were captured by the ones they were with." Do you agree with General Rose's assessment, that many of the UNMOs were not technically competent?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part I would agree with, but if I could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To say that the UNMO reports were completely useless I think is an over-characterisation of the statements of those reports. I think some were useful. Those UNMOs that came from countries with professional forces, with professional trained officers, Scandinavian countries, UK, US, Canada, had better-quality reports that were used by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assessment that UNMOs sided with whomever they were situated with and that reports were based on what local commanders told them rather than what they observed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some examples, but it was not endemic across all the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now call up your 1997 statement again, that's 1D457, and page 14 in the English, page 15 in the B/C/S. And I will be focussing on the middle of the page, sir, which is the portion that is the UNMOs. And this is the 1997 report, sir, not the hard copy. So it's on the screen on the right-hand side. And the part I'm interested in says quote -- is under the title "UNMOs": "UNMOs were attached to the sector. In theory, they were supposed to report to the sector, whereas in reality the sector did not use them. They were inconsistent, unreliable, and, in fact, they reported first to Zagreb, which wasn't of such use to us. When an incident did happen, if the UNMOs were first on the scene, the sector would try to get as much information form them as possible but would then send in our backup team. We relied on our own LOs, our units, rather than the UNMOs. My bosses, both sector commanders, were cordial with them, but they used their own resources." First of all, sir, with the comments that you made in relation to General Rose's proofing statement and this paragraph that I've read from your 1999 [sic] statement, do they truthfully and accurately reflect the totality of your evidence as to the UNMOs that you saw during your tenure in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, as I said, that they were inconsistent and many of them unreliable. There were exceptions within them that they -- some of the reports they had were useful. And in situations where they did arrive first, a pair of inconsistent, unreliable eyes is better than no eyes whatsoever, which was reinforced and backed up - as I say - by the troops that the sector commander had under his command. An imperfect tool is better than no tool.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that as far as the UNMOs were concerned, their degree of reliability depended on the nationality of the particular UNMOs, what nation they came from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that there was a national bias of sorts within Sector Sarajevo as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me try and clarify that by looking at, again, your 1997 statement which is on the screen, and if we turn to page 4 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. I'm referring to the section that is in the third paragraph from the top that I will read out for you, sir, and then you can follow along from your -- from the screen. "In Sector Sarajevo, there were two staff systems working, the UN and the French. It was the French staff who effectively ran Sector Sarajevo during the majority of the meaningful work. The UN officers in the headquarters were essential 'window dressing.' The French also wrote and maintained their own national reports. This process became more complicated when the Russians imposed a Chief of Staff of their own on the Sector, but he was marginalised by the French." First of all, sir, can I ask you if you stand by the foregoing selection I have jest read as being truthful and accurate as to the situation in Sector Sarajevo Command during the time that you were the MA?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That situation -- and I stand by my statement that the core of this headquarters was French, they knew each other, they were professional soldiers. They could work very well together because they understood each other. They could work quickly, efficiently, effectively, and other officers who were clipped on to their -- the core of this headquarters had to catch up to where the French were. They were very professional and very good. In a situation where there was a civil war going on, they had to get action done quickly to protect and achieve the mandate of the UN. That said, not all the officers who came in from other countries in the UN were as capable as the professional force. And also when are you in the midst of operations and you interpose a different nationality, the Chief of Staff, he just had to catch up speed and the French were moving quite quickly because at this time tensions were rising, activity on the ground -- conflict was rising, and things had to be done. So the most expeditious way of doing it was -- quite frankly, was the core way was with the French and up at General Rose and General Smith's headquarters a lot of -- a lot of work fell onto British soldiers too because that's just where the core was and Dutch and Canadians. And that's just how things worked to get things done on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so you say that the Chief of Staff was -- had to catch up. In fact, wasn't he basically bypassed or marginalised in the process, cut out of the equation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, because it came from a complete different culture, a completely different system, that he had to find time to get himself up to speed. He arrived at a time where, in fact, combat activities were fairly intense, and it took him a while to get things going.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you verify for us that the French at Sector Sarajevo maintained a secret red file of information that was for the viewing of only French personnel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every nation has their own national command chains with their own national reports. The French with their files were no different than any other nation. We all reported back to our national capitals as representatives, so they had their own system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we have the 1997 statement before us, I'd like to turn to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S of the same. And I'd like to ask you, sir, about the last paragraph in the English, which is on the right-hand side of your screen, and your statement records as follows: "Protest letters were done and I drafted letters of protest for the commanders. The commander would tell me what he wanted, what the slant was, and I would draft the letters and give them back to him. Sometimes these letters really seemed like for the sake of form. You always had to be careful with the letters you wrote, because they could turn things back at you." Now, General Fraser, first of all, can you confirm that these words from your 1997 statement are truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you, this paragraph uses the terminology "what the slant was." Am I to take it from that that the sector commander would direct you to slant a particular letter either for or against a particular side, i.e., the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He, in fact, would tell me what the theme and what the facts and what type of message he wanted to relay to the affected party. We treated both sides equally and fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "the letters really seemed like for the sake of form," does that mean that decisions had already been made and it didn't matter what either of the warring factions did in response to the letter, UNPROFOR already had a course of action determined?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, it was more a comment on the warring factions despite our protestations of an incident that the warring factions in many cases just ignored our -- our protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to now go into private session to discuss the topic raised yesterday in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday at transcript page 5805 you talked of freedom of movement for humanitarian aid. I would like to turn to your consolidated statement which you have in front of you, P576, and I'm interested in the 13th page in English and the 14th page in the B/C/S. And I'm interested in paragraph 42, which is the second paragraph from the top in the English. Here, you assert that the Serbs would rachet up pressure by interfering with the humanitarian aid. Now, I want to confirm first - I think it's back at paragraph 14 of your statement, but I don't think we need to turn to there unless you disagree with me - but the mandate of -- one of the mandates of UN Sector Sarajevo included ensuring freedom of movement for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the impartially of the UN Sector Sarajevo mission as to both sides in the conflict was essential to the performance and success of the mission as to ensuring the movement of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, what you've described as racheting up the pressure, in fact, isn't this true that the Serbs had the legitimate concern to ensure that humanitarian aid being transported was not misused to clandestinely transport either military weapons or ammunition or other military supplies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in so far as the UN Sector Sarajevo's mission dealt with the movement of humanitarian aid, did Sector Sarajevo take steps to ensure that the aid convoys or transports were not misused in a manner to transport military materials or hardware for either side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the UN did try to make sure that those convoys were only for humanitarian aid, as under the auspices of UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which organisation's responsibility was it to inspect cargo to ensure that there was no contraband of a military nature onboard?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, a number of agencies looked at it: The UNHCR, who had the overall responsibility for the convoys, and then the military aspect of the UN. We also made sure that -- you know, through our sources that those convoys were what they said they were, and that the freedom of movement was for what it -- for the benefit of the civilians inside Sarajevo and the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the inspection of these convoys by the Serbs, by the VRS, was a legitimate and appropriate function to determine if weapons or munitions or other contraband was present in the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, but it never materialised that way. Our experience was - as I stand by my statement - the freedom of movement and those convoys, Serbs overplayed that comment that you just gave, that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you help me to understand your answer. You say "it never materialised that way." Are you saying that there were never weapons found or military supplies found on aid convoys during the time-period that you were the MA at Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall of -- military weapons being found on -- on convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if weapons were found on convoys, this would give the Serbs very legitimate gripes with the UN and would give them a justification to be wary of future convoys and/or limit the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a hypothetical question that I just answered. I did not have any information of any contraband on those convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that during the time-period that you were with Sector Sarajevo, there were some serious allegations that UN personnel were even actively engaged in the smuggling of weapons or other criminal activity on the side of the Bosnian Muslims [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbs"]?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one incident that I know of and it was a fallacious allegation of the UN transporting some ammunition, which was for our own purposes and not for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I ask you a question -- you switched in -- in -- among -- after one question you were talking whether it was legitimate to inspect convoys. And then the next question, you asked - that was the hypothetical question - whether they could limit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I -- it's not entirely clear what position of the Defence is, that they were entitled to ask for these convoys to be inspected on the presence of military material; or whether they could limit it, limiting being a bit of an ambiguous expression. It could also be you can do only two a week or once a month or -- it's unclear to me. You used different language, and I would like to understand fully what made you do this or whether it is indicative of the position of the Defence in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I basically was talking about the inspection regimes. But I do know from prior witnesses that there were issues of convoys that did not have the proper documentation or were not given advance notice, could not be verified, and therefore would be limited without being inspected until the paperwork was available. So that would be my answer to that, although I was asking this witness about just the inspection regimes. So I did misspeak when I added the -- limiting to the second hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you now use the word "would be limited without being inspected." So the position at this moment - and that's the underlying thought of these questions - is that if there are legitimate concerns about weapons being smuggled that the Serbs were entitled to inspection; and if the paperwork was not correct, to then stop the convoy until the inspection had been complete and the paperwork was complete as well. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would be my position that either side, as I understand it, the Croats in -- in the other side of the country also had the same problems with weapons being smuggled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether others had similar problems -- my question is, because you -- these questions were focussed on the Serbs in Sarajevo. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish the factual backdrop that is relevant to the time-period in the indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I asked you whether that was the Defence position. If you didn't limit it in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say -- I take it that you're trying to give evasive answers, where you actually want to say: I want to discuss this with lead counsel, isn't it? Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether you do it or not is not my concern. But why not say immediately: I would have to discuss that with lead counsel before I answer your question? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I have to intervene only in regard of the transcript. Your Honour, if I may just intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have to intervene in regard with the transcript. Line -- page 17, line 3, says "Bosnian Serbs" and should be "Bosnian Muslims," and it changes the question drastically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check one second. You said ... Could you again give the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 17, 3. Let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Last two words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it to be "Bosnian Muslims." That's -- I don't know whether -- Mr. Ivetic, I don't think, as a matter of fact, that -- let me read again to you the question that was put and that you started to answer. Mr. Ivetic asked you: "Am I correct that during the time-period that you were with Sector Sarajevo there was some serious allegations that UN personnel were even actively engaged in the smuggling of weapons or other criminal activity on the side of the Bosnian" -- Did you then understand that the question was about Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you could just clarify which side you wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. You started answering. You said: "There was only one incident I know of." Did you understand the question to be about Sector Sarajevo siding with Bosnian Muslims? If that's how you understand it, please, tell us; if you understood it as the Sector Sarajevo siding with the Bosnian Serbs, tell us as well, so that we better understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My under -- I interpreted and my understanding was siding with the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was intended. That is how I understood it. That is how everyone apparently understood it. So only one incident was -- one incident you knew of Bosnian Muslims involved in this type of activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think that clarifies the matter. Whether it was a transcript error or whether you misspoke, Mr. Ivetic, seems to be of less relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was a transcript error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think it was a transcript error, yes. I leave it to the parties whether to take further action or whether we just accept this to be the case, where the understanding is common among all of us in this courtroom, witness, parties, and Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to turn to 1D00453, and I will be looking at page 40 in e-court of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, while we wait for it to come up on the screen, I can advise you this is the transcript of 18 October 2010 from the Karadzic proceedings. And at page 40 we're looking at line 22. And I will read for you what is recorded as having been said and then ask for your input. "Q. Thank you. In our conversation, you confirmed that you had knowledge -- or, rather, the UN had knowledge about the existence of the black market and the involvement on UN personnel in such transactions, and that there were even some investigations carried out about that." And if we can go to the next page for the continuation, at the top. "A. The UN were conducting investigations of allegations of black-marketeering by the UN, and this was taken very seriously and investigated by a task force that came out of Zagreb. "Q. There were even criminal vehicles that were blown up illegally, and those were vehicles [as interpreted] by those who were trying to prevent this. A French officer who was trying to prevent this was blown up; isn't that right? "Let me rephrase this question. Is it correct that a vehicle of the commander of a French platoon, who was trying to prevent this black-marketeering, was blown up, and that this had to do with his activities aimed at countering the black-market activities? "A. There was a French military police platoon commander who had his vehicle booby-trapped with a bomb. He was in the process of investigation -- investigating black-marketeering, and he did come to us and we put him and the proper police authorities on to the allegations of black-marketeering that he was looking into. "Q. At our meeting, you claimed that the booby-trapping of this vehicle could have to do possibly with his activities against black-marketeering; is that correct? "A. That's what I said, yes. "Q. Thank you. There was also UN personnel that was involved in prostitution rings in Sarajevo; is that correct? "A. I've heard of those allegations and any -- any allegations that we would have heard about, we would have brought the proper investigative authorities in to address those allegations." First of all, sir, would you agree with me this selection of your testimony from the Karadzic case is both truthful and accurate as the matters you were asked about there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you remember, how many of these type of investigations into black-market smuggling or prostitution did the UN undertake during the time-period that you were the MA at Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector commander convened one major investigation in-house and tasked -- the headquarters in Zagreb had a major task force that came down to investigate black marketeering as a whole. So those -- those two I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any UN officers or employees ever disciplined for their role in any such black-market activities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time that I was there, no, because the investigations were ongoing when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the matters that you were talking about in this section complained of or brought to the attention of the UN by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of the transcript, I'd like to also ask you about the follow-up questions that you had. It starts at page -- at line 1, I apologise. "Q. Thank you. You said, during our conversation, that the UN CIVPOL carried out a major investigation into the smuggling activities involving ammunition, weapons, vehicles, fuel, people, identity cards, and alcohol; is this correct? "A. There was -- this was part of the UN task force on black-marketeering, and the sector conducted at least one major investigation on allegations of black-marketeering. "Q. And this had to do with the smuggling of the articles that I just referred to and that you also referred to during our conversation; is that correct? "A. That is correct. "Q. Thank you. You also agreed that because of this, Serbs did have reason to be cautious in approving the entry of convoys into Sarajevo, in light of the [sic] black-marketeering; is that correct? "A. I did not agree to that. I would say that, in fact, black-marketeering was an issue that all warring factions had to deal with. And the UN took it very seriously and dealt with it, and we raised those issues with the appropriate side. "Q. But you would agree, would you not, that the Serbs had reasons for increased caution and control of everything that was coming into Sarajevo, in light of this information? "A. I would not agree that the Serbs had to have increased control. I would say that the Serbs, in co-operation with the UN, should have looked at black-marketeering and to respect the UN mandate for freedom of movement." First of all, sir, can you confirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this section of your testimony from the Karadzic case as to this -- these topics?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. They're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say here that you think the Serbs should have co-operated with the UN to look into black-marketeering. So I want to ask you: In regards to the UN task force that you identify, were the Serbs included as part of that task force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You would have to ask the -- the organisation that was running the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which organisation ran the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNCIVPOL from UN headquarters out of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo ever, in writing, acknowledge the serious problem of any black-marketeering or weapons smuggling, let alone invite the Serbs to take part in any kind of joint efforts to try and stop this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't recall of any -- any letters that went out on that subject, other than the -- the one in-house investigation we had on black-marketeering.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're at the one-hour mark. We could take a break, if Your Honours would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to be a suitable moment. We will take a break of 20 minutes, but only after you've left the courtroom, Mr. Fraser. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while he is coming in, could I just address briefly a procedural issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On -- a week ago Tuesday the Prosecution filed its submissions on the admissibility of the associated exhibits with respect to Mr. Roy Thomas, and earlier this week the Defence filed a response. And I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution won't be filing any reply to that. So if that expedites the rendering of a decision, that would assist us in terms of identifying exhibits for future witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While the exception would be that you would intend to file a reply, whereas the normal situation is as you describe it now -- I'm saying this because the Chamber has some concern about requests for replies to be filed, seems to become now and then a routine where it should not become a routine. Having said this, we can continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But thank you anyway, Ms. Bolton, for informing the Chamber. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I forgot to ask you earlier, do you recall the name of the Russian Sector Sarajevo Chief of Staff whom we discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. We also talked earlier about how the French were running the affairs of Sector Sarajevo, and I want to take a look at another document, 1D474. And as we wait for it to come up, I believe this is a 12 May 1994 report of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps sent to the Main Staff of the VRS; and if this date is accurate, this is about a month into your tour of duty at Sector Sarajevo. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 1 in the B/C/S at the bottom and page 3 in the English. And we'll see here, sir, the information that: "A BOV" armoured combat vehicle "of the French Battalion was stopped at the check-point in Kasindolska Street. And during the check it was established that it was transporting seven cases of shells for the 82 MM MB" mortar "allegedly for their units in Rajlovac. "Verification established that they had not even disclosed they possess a weapon of" the above "calibre and the further resolution of this problem is in progress. "We had two members of UNPROFOR travelling in an off-road vehicle without permission in the z/o of the 3 Spbr on the route Kosevo towards Visojevici from where then intercepted and turned back." First of all, General Fraser what can you tell us about this incident, where it would appear that the French Battalion was transporting mines -- mortar mines for weapons that were not listed as being part of -- or not declared, I guess, as part of the arsenal in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were moving the ammunition for their own purposes. And the weapons systems, whether or not they were disclosed to the Serbs or not, were used for the French to prosecute their operations under the UN mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The document says that "further resolution of this problem is in progress." Do you know if there was a -- joint efforts by the Serbs and the UNPROFOR to resolve this issue?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the incident that I mentioned earlier, where the Serbs raised it against the UN. The UN, we - to the best of my knowledge - acknowledged that this was ammunition for our own purposes, nothing else. And I would also add that I don't think under the mandate we needed permission to be travelling. Again, that was an example of freedom -- restriction of our freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it often the case that French units were accused of engaging in smuggling activities on behalf of the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At transcript page 5809 and through 5810 yesterday, you talked about P587, Mladic's order to restrict UNPROFOR and aid convoys. If we can call that up, first of all. It should be P587. And just to be clear, by the time that this was issued, the 10th of April, 1994, UNPROFOR had just bombed the Serbs; is that accurate -- pardon me, NATO had just bombed the Serbs. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just go to the next page? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If another party bombs a country - let's say Canada - is that considered an act of aggression or an act of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- are you asking for a legal opinion on this matter, Mr. Ivetic, or ... Because isn't it true that the prohibition of aggression is a rather complex matter? It took them decades to define "aggression" at the United Nations. Isn't it true there is a kind of a tension between bombing in self-defence, which would make it an act of war; bombing as an aggressive act. It is a rather complex legal matter you're raising with the witness. So would you please, instead of putting this question in such a general way, further explore the details of the assumptions on which such a question necessarily is based, context.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a gentleman here who, based upon his experience as a Canadian -- member of the armed forces of Canada as a general, has offered opinions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- for the Prosecution on these very same topics as to how to qualify actions of the parties on the ground in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I'm asking him now a hypothetical: If anyone, a force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there already. All those opinions -- and perhaps needless to say that the Chamber is very cautious in making a distinction between what a witness testified in terms of facts he observed, reports he received, et cetera -- and let me be very candid to you, it was the last time during the last break that we were discussing the issue of opinions against facts. This witness, when you asked him for opinion several times, reduced your questions to the facts he observed. So he apparently is very aware of that as well. But at least that was all in the context of a factual situation which existed in Sarajevo. You are now going one step further, asking opinion without any context, apart from the general legal context. That does not assist the Chamber. And whether the witness should be reminded of his duties or not, that's a different matter. But the Chamber primarily wants to receive evidence which assists it in performing its task. Could you please keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Allow me to try to and give some context. If we look at this document, P587 - and I believe you have a second page in English -- yes, you do - and if we read items 1 through 3, and 5, as a soldier, as a general in the -- retired in the Canadian Armed Forces, do these items, 1, 2, 3, and 5, appear to be normal and what you would expect as a response to an armed force being bombed by another armed force?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this document, in relation to what was happening on the ground, no. I had not arrived on the ground, but I was briefed on what was happening on the ground when I got there. And the warnings went out to the Serbian forces to cease their operations or consequences would happen because of the civilians in the enclave; and, as a result, NATO was asked and attacked a target on the ground. And this was the reaction to that set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you through it step by step. Since we have number 5 up on the screen, let's start with number 5. Are you telling me, as a military officer, as a general in the Canadian Armed Forces, that it is not expected or normal after being bombed by a military force to instruct your forces to fire independently in case of self-defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that we are, again, going into a hypothetical situation of what occur if one country were attacked by another country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think at this moment you either object to the question and then give the precise reasons for that, or let Mr. Ivetic finish his question. He is now not in general terms talk anymore. He is focussing specifically on what we find in paragraph 5. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you asked me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I gave a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you asked me to articulate my -- whether I was objecting or not, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I said that you had an opportunity to object on the question on specific grounds, and you started giving all kind of explanations. And then I ruled that Mr. Ivetic can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I object on the grounds of relevance for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, isn't it clear to you that I gave a ruling? I told you that twice. Allow Mr. Ivetic to proceed. And that I do not expect you at that moment to just ignore what I said. Is that clear to you? I hope it is. Is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I understand you made a ruling and I was simply putting the Prosecution's position on the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for further explanations. I'm asking whether it's clear what I said to you, that once I gave a ruling that Mr. Ivetic may proceed, that you should not - certainly not twice - ignore that ruling. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have difficulties in admitting things, isn't it? We noticed that yesterday as well when you were late with your disclosure; you tried to soften it. Instead of saying: Apologies to the Defence. How can we remedy the situation we created? That is a comment I give now I refrained from giving yesterday. I leave it to that. And Mr. Ivetic is now allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, may I have the opportunity to respond to the comment you made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you do not have and it's now the third time that you apparently do not understand what a ruling in court means. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Are you telling me, as a military officer, as a general in the Canadian Armed Forces, that it is not expected or normal after being bombed by a military force to instruct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I interrupt you. Mr. Lukic, if you want to briefly consult with Mr. Mladic, you have an opportunity to do so. Keep your voices low, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think for the sake of clarity, I'll start at the beginning again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling me as a military officer, as a general in the Canadian Armed Forces, that it is not expected or normal after being bombed by a military force to instruct your forces to fire independently in case of self-defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Section 5 of this document and what you said, that is legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the previous page, which I believe would be page 2 in the English, and if we could focus in on number 1. As a military officer, as a general in the Canadian Armed Forces, is it not expected or normal, after being bombed by a military force, to instruct all commands and units of your army to be at full combat-readiness, to suspend leave of soldiers, and to call back soldiers who are already on leave?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this document, no. We were not in war with the Serbian forces. We were there as -- under the UN mandate, and our issues were not with the Serbian forces per se. And what that suggests to me -- that statement in and by itself, fine. I have no issues with that. But the allegation that you are giving me is that we were going in conflict with the Serbian forces; that was not our mandate. And I want to talk about this -- this document in the context of what was going on, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- make one very brief comment. In your previous question you introduced an element of self-defence which does not appear in the document; it's your interpretation, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does appear in the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Number 5. I'm sorry, it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's -- then I missed that. Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be the last line of item number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me check then. It's now on my screen. Let me have a look. Oh you -- yes, now I -- let me just check then. One second, please. Yes, in case of self-defence. If there would be any -- of course, that this requires to further define whether there exist or there could exist a self-defence situation. But that is an element which we have to consider in this context, Mr. Ivetic. But you're right, that's what the document says. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about the context of events. Am I correct that the entirety of your mission in Bosnia, the Bosnian Muslim side was continually asking for military intervention from outside on its behalf against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked and did not receive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Under that context, as a military commander, where the other side is asking for military intervention, there has just been a form of military action against you. Are you saying that it would be illogical to call up your forces and have them ready for combat-readiness, as a precaution?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement by itself, I -- I have -- there is no problem with that statement, what they were asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the prior page and look at item number 2, do you have a problem with what is being asked for in item number 2, again, in the context of the situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a problem with it, in the sense that it's somewhat ambiguous. They are to fire -- to be ready to fire immediately on targets in air-space, because under normal circumstances the fact that NATO aircraft are flying are not a threat to either side, but again the actions on the ground actually put the Serbian forces into a self-defence mode because of a failure to communicate with the UN and stop what the UN was asking the Serbians on the ground to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the context that I answer your question, that when I see they are to be ready to fire immediately on targets in the air-space --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Read the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Fire on receiving an order to do so from the KM, command -- command post, of the GS VRS or independently in the case of an attack from air-space."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is very clearly limited to "in case of an attack" or on order; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That attack was precipitated by the actions of the ground forces and the warning went out before that. That is the context that I answer that -- to that particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at item number 4. It is specific about how the persons to be detained are to be treated. As a soldier, if you were to put yourself on the receiving end of a bombing, would you not agree that it would be prudent, in terms of safety -- and that members of the organisation or force that has just taken hostile action against you be detained and kept in a safe place, would you give a similar order if you were bombed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, that section 4 says: "Immediately block all UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations' convoys and their teams which happen to be in the RS, Republika Srpska, territory." There's no reason for doing that. First of all, it's not even specific to the area of conflict - it says "the general entire area" - which is a violation of the UN mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to: "Remove and secure the convoys and bring the personnel and secure them in a safe place. Do not treat them roughly in the process." It's heartening to have to tell people not to treat them roughly. You shouldn't have to say at that. It is a common course --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, General, I put to you that in the military sense a military commander who does not encourage his forces to abide by the rules of engagement and by the laws of war is perhaps negligent in his duties, as case law has found. But I would like to ask you, sir, what is the standard operating procedure or protocol of the Canadian Armed Forces upon an attack by a third party as to nationals of that third party that are armed and on the territory of Canada?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Objection, relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I objected on the grounds of relevance what he would do on the basis of a Canadian -- sorry, we're missing part of the question which had to do with what he would do in a situation as a Canadian soldier under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to withdraw the question and move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I made the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when you addressed the witness several times as a Canadian with a lot of military experience, I understood this to be mainly to refer to the experience of the witness rather than being a Canadian. But one of the things that -- the situation we are finding in this document is one which is complex, that is, that the starting point is that there are NATO attacks, and it gives instructions as to how to treat UNPROFOR people, humanitarian organisations, what to do with that. In order to assist the Chamber rather than asking the questions you have put, it would require a thorough analysis of the starting point, who is there, which party is linked to whom, if there is any legitimate reason to respond or to take action, against which party should that be done, or against which party it would be legitimate to do that, that requires first an analysis rather than to focus on the few lines of the -- this order, this very urgent order. That would assist the Chamber more if we would have that analysis. Whether you want to make an analysis with the witness, yes or no, we leave that to you, but that is a comment on your line of questioning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. I thought it was in the statement, but perhaps I'll just ask the witness to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The NATO bombings against the Serbs was at the request of your superior officers in UNPROFOR; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that that -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is one of the examples. Do you have any authority, what military action can take against a party who has asked another military force to take military action, where the party requesting it doesn't have the means perhaps or not sufficient means to do that? And that is -- these are all very complex matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber is very much willing to analyse them in detail together with the parties. But, again, I'm asking: Is there any authority you could give us so as to assist us in understanding the real issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this stage, no, Your Honours. I was merely attempting to point out that the one explanation offered but the Office of the Prosecution on this witness in presenting this document is not clear-cut nor the only conclusion that can be reached for the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is your purpose, then you have drawn our attention to that element. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to discussion sniping a bit more in detail. And if we can turn to P576, your consolidated statement -- pardon me. For your information, I'm talking about paragraphs 56 and onwards of your consolidated statement, but I'd actually like to first start with 1D423, which, again, is the information sheet of the discussions of General Rose with the Prosecution. And I would like to turn to page 3 of that document, of where -- where General Rose is -- is reported as saying: "I am sure that the Serbs were firing at the trams but I believe Ganic also organised his secret police to snipe trams. His sniper unit sniped so that the angle of the shot matched the direction of the [sic] Serb line. During long cease-fires, I think that Ganic and the Muslims ... were responsible for breaking the cease-fire. This kept the tension." Sir, did you have the same information that Bosnian Presidency secret police snipers were sniping at the trams in a way to mimic the direction of the Serb line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to return to your 1997 statement to the OTP, that's 1D457.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the information sheet or the proofing notes - I take it that you're talking about General Rose - do you intend to tender that? Because there seems to be a quite a few sweeping statements in there which may be perfectly right but which might need further analysis to better assess the -- if I could say the quality of those statements. And of course, I do not know, is General Rose on the witness list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can deal with it once he is there, and I -- I'd forgotten about that. But since you refer to it several times, I wondered how we could process that instead of reading only small portions to have a bit of a better idea. Because we were able to read a few more lines which may require further attention as to the accuracy of the observations made by General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd be happy to tender it now, if the Prosecution has no objection, since we have used it I think already five times in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour. I would prefer to deal with the issue of the context in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's wait until we have re-examination. One of the reasons I was just trying to -- it was on the screens so I read a few lines and I saw, for example, that General Rose gave a statement which may be easy to verify, that more people died in 1994 by crime in Washington than people died in Sarajevo. That's a, I would say, a very verifiable fact on its accuracy, and that trigged me to ask you, Ms. Bolton, whether we should have that in evidence. But we'll wait for Ms. Bolton. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can have 1D457 called up on the screen. And if we can look at page 11 in both the English and the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm focussing now, sir, on the first paragraph, or the start of the first subparagraph under the heading "Sniping," wherein you state: "Both sides conducted sniper activity. It was used mainly as a terrorist type of activity. During my tenure in Sarajevo, sniping ended up in a tit-for-tat type of exchange. If a Muslim shot a Serb, the Serbs would say they'd shoot 10 Muslims. Both sides were indiscriminate and shot men, women, and children." Sir, can you confirm the selection I have just read from your 1997 statement as being truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is the crux of your -- well, strike that. Would you agree with me that the party that benefitted most politically from these sniping incidents was the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I would like to object to that question on the basis that it calls for an opinion in an area where, as a military person, we wouldn't expect him to have the ability to provide opinion evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is sustained. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on Snipers Alley for just a bit, am I correct that the Bosnian Muslims also had snipers situated and active in this area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 5801 you talked of the Serbs having reluctance to protect their trolley-bus line. I'd like to focus on Snipers Alley, and am I correct that UNPROFOR attempted to erect sniper barriers to negate the ability of persons to be shot in the so-called snipers area -- Snipers Alley? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that the Bosnian Muslim authorities in Sarajevo either objected or did not agree with the erection of all the sniper barriers that the UN was willing to put up?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I do not recall -- recall them objecting or not agreeing to the erection of those barriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 1D454, and if we can have page 26 in e-court. This is the transcript, I believe, from the Karadzic proceedings. It is. If we can have page 26 -- well, yes, 26. And if we can focus on item -- line number 5 and the question that was posed to you, sir, is as follows: "Q. Thank you. Is it correct that the authorities in the Muslim part of Sarajevo did not agree, and that this effort to erect barricades was halted? You can look at page 24 of your statement, if you like: [In English] 'The sector tried to improve the situation as regards the barriers by putting more.' [No interpretation]. [In English] 'Sometimes the city wanted it; sometimes they didn't.' "A. I won't dispute that. And in every case, as I recall, the safety of the citizens was paramount, and we would do what we thought was right to protect citizens."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when you are reading, your speed of speech goes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Do I need to repeat? COURT REPORTER: Wait, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise to Madam Court Reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, does this selection from the Karadzic transcript refresh your recollection as to whether the Muslim authorities did not agree to all the barriers that the UN intended to put up in Snipers Alley?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refreshes my memory, and you can appreciate that after these years not all the details would be immediately at the tip of my tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I thought you said this refers to Snipers Alley, but does this excerpt here refer to Snipers Alley?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it does in the prior page of this transcript. But if we look at the top of -- the top of this page, items 1 through 3, the answer of the witness upon the question is: "We had a concerted effort to erect barricades to increase safety throughout the city where they were needed, not just simply on Snipers Alley." So he's talking Snipers Alley and other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So the answer is general, really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- if I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement that I have there in front of me. I cannot recall all the specific details about what the city did or did not agree to. The UN had a concerted effort to have a passive barrier on Sniper Alley which was the main effort. The city was in agreement of that because we had a substantial anti-sniping task force on that area. A UN soldier was killed in -- there; another one was shot and severely wounded there. This was the main effort, and I do not recall specific details if the city ever objected on Sniper Alley of the -- of the measures that we took. But I'll stand by, as a general statement, maybe the city did not agree with all the places and it was a matter of priority of where do we put our -- our resources?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can turn to 65 ter number 10096. This is an UNPROFOR BH command sitrep, which I think we will see is dated the 27th of February, 1995. First of all, sir, looking at the first page, are you able to confirm that this is, in fact, a BH command sitrep dated 27 February 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have page 10 of the document in e-court. And I would focus on the part that starts: "Assessment." It's the third paragraph from the top, and I'd like to go through the first -- I guess, it's the sentence that deals with: "Although the number of firing incidents decreased, tension is likely to remain at an elevated level following the shooting incidents by uncontrolled elements at the airport and against the tram." Do you have knowledge and would you agree that during the time-period that you were -- during this time-period, excuse me, February 1995, the UN found that uncontrolled elements were sometimes the source of the fire being experienced?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The description of uncontrolled elements was a term used by both warring factions to justify why actions took place. And in the context of this assessment, I'm not aware of the drafter or who released it, whether or not that person is just using the terms given to the UN by the effective warring faction or, in fact, if that was the case. So if you could rephrase your question within that context, it would probably help me. Because this is the first time I have seen this report, but I do know the term was used liberally to try explain situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up, again, 1D454, and if we can turn to page 33 in e-court and perhaps if we can have the English of the -- well, I'm sorry. Never mind. Page 33 in e-court of 1D454. This is during the Karadzic proceedings and is transcript page 8129 of that trial, and I'd like to focus on lines 20 through 25 of this page, which should be at the bottom. And it would appear to me, sir, that, here Mr. Karadzic was asking about this very same document in so far as lines 20 to 22 appear to have the same text that I have just read to you and the question that was posed to you at line 23 is: "Do you agree that the United Nations established that there was fire opened by uncontrolled elements? "A. There was a degree of uncontrolled elements, yes." First of all, sir, are you able to tell us when you gave this answer in the Karadzic proceedings, what was your understanding of "uncontrolled elements" that the UN had established?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a degree of uncontrolled elements, but it was also a pivot that both warring factions tried to use multiple times. The situation on the ground was never black and white; it was always grey. Notwithstanding that, the UN -- we spent a lot of time trying to advise both parties to control the situation because the people most adversely affected were non-combatants, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We talked about Brigadier Fikret of the ABiH around the airport area. Would you consider him to be an uncontrolled element?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. No, he was under -- he was under control by Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how numerous the personnel under his command were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that he commanded a brigade during the time that I was there, and it was the brigade in -- just -- just at the foot of the Igman Mounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 66 of your consolidated statement - that would be, again, P576, for you to follow along, sir, in the hard copy, and it's the nineteenth page in the English - you talk about how trams were a favourite target of the Serb snipers and that in your opinion, trams could not be hit by accident. In this regard I'd like to take a look at 65 ter number 10096 again. That was the sitrep of the 27th of February, 1995. And if we could have page 9 of 10096 in e-court. I'd like to focus on the reporting of an incident from Sector Sarajevo. At page 9 it says: "A tram travelling between BP 90593 [sic] and BP 907592 was fired at, reportedly resulting in one confirmed civilian casualty and possibly three other casualties. The confirmed casualty suffered a leg injury. The estimated origin of fire was BP 907589. Tramway service ceased following the incident. During the same time-period, both sides were involved in a fire-fight 300 metres away in the area of the Vrbanja Bridge (BP 912589). An MG CFV has been attributed to both the BiH and BSA for the event overall." Now, sir, first of all, MG CFV, would that be a registered violation of the -- of the cease-fire agreement that was in -- in place at the time-period?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says a machine-gun cease-fire violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- this all started with a quote from paragraph 66, Mr. Ivetic. You quoted it as --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That the trams could not be hit by accident, I believe, was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What it says is that: "It's extremely unlikely that a professional sniper would hit a tram by accident given their skill levels. Trams were a favourite target of Bosnian Serb snipers." Let's put the question directly to the witness. Would you exclude for the possibility that a tram could be hit by accident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not exclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're saying in paragraph 66 is that the frequency of trams being hit by snipers made you believe that they were specifically targeted. Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, I believe this incident that is discussed in this document was G-14 which has been removed from the indictment, but let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the trams in Sarajevo and this particular tram line, isn't it true that it ran very close to areas of active combat between the Serb and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that it did, and I also would reinforce that the UN, in its reporting, did acknowledge when there were actions between two warring factions and there was collateral damage and injuries, as it reported here, "we said so." But going back to paragraph 66 of my statement, I'm talking about a sniper, and snipers do not use machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During your time-period at UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo, were you aware that the ABiH used several high-rise buildings for their snipers, including the Unis building and the Executive Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of that. And we protested that when there were examples of that against the Serbian side, against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to 1D457, and again this is your 1997 statement, which -- on the screen it will be page 18 in the English, page 20 in the -- in the Serb. And this is going to be the last paragraph on page 18 that I'm asking you about, sir. And it begins as follows: "On September 18, Rose was not in Sarajevo. Soubirou was the acting commander. There was another shooting incident. The Muslims fired four mortars out of the city, and the Bosnian Serbs replied by firing into the city. At the same time, the Bosnian Serbs threatened to take their weapons out of Lukavica to counter what the Muslims had just done. Incoming rounds continued over some time. We tried to contact everyone to tell them to stop. Rose sent a fax to both warring parties and the press complaining about the violation, and how it was the Bosnian Muslims had begun. Rose stated that if they didn't stop, the UN would attack each side equally with air." First of all, sir, is this selection from your 1997 statement truthful and accurate as to this occurrence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the action of the Bosnian Muslims was a violation of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement and weapons exclusion zone that was in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was and that's why we protested against the Muslims for doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR actually go ahead and ask NATO to strike either the -- strike the Bosnian Muslims on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not escalate to that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But the Serbs were bombed on the 22nd September, several days later, by NATO at the request of UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During your entire time-period at UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo, did the UN -- the UNPROFOR mission ever request NATO to perform air-strikes and bomb the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are approximately at. We had a bit of a late start. We take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Fraser, could you follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to, at this time, take a look at a document from the day before the 22 September bombing of the Serbs by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 1D471 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it, I'll just introduce, sir, that I think we'll see this to be a report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the VRS Main Staff dated 21 September 1994. And if we can look at the second page, I guess, in English --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought my friend said this was a document from the 21st of September. This appears to be from March 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, yes. And it's also not, I think, what you said was a report but, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 1D470. And I thank Ms. Bolton for pointing out the error. As I was -- I would have spent much more time looking through the document to find the selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can focus on the part, sir, here, where it's at the beginning where it says: "Any agreements with the Muslim forces or warnings by General Rose are pointless. They fire artillery pieces with calibre larger than 12.7 mm from the exclusion zone on our positions and settlements, also in the exclusion zone."
